A.q: Which set lists only functions of the skeletal system?
options: Producing heat, generating locomotion, moving the limbs
Storing minerals, forming blood, anchoring muscles
Filtering lymph, housing immune cells, clearing particles
Exchanging gases, regulating pressure and heart rate
A.explain: The skeletal system stores minerals, forms blood cells, and gives muscles a surface to attach to. Heat and movement are muscular, filtering is lymphatic, and gas exchange and pressure are respiratory and cardiovascular.

A.q: Which directional term is paired with its correct reference?
A.explain: Medial means close to the midline. Proximal is near the origin, distal is away from it, and lateral is away from the midline.

A.q: Which directional pair is defined correctly?
options: Superior: away from head; inferior: toward
A.explain: Anterior is the front (ventral) and posterior the back (dorsal). Superior is toward the head and inferior away from it.

A.q: How do compact and spongy (cancellous) bone differ?
options: Compact: solid, exterior; spongy: mesh-like, interior
Compact: mesh-like, interior; spongy: solid, exterior
Compact: stores blood cells; spongy: anchors muscles
Compact: makes blood; spongy: lubricates joints
A.explain: Compact bone is tight, solid, and forms the exterior; spongy bone is mesh-like and forms the interior around the medullary cavity.

A.q: Compare red and yellow bone marrow.

steps.prompt: Which marrow produces the blood components?
Red marrow makes blood. Which marrow fills the body at birth?
All marrow is red at birth. What converts part to yellow?

A.explain: Red marrow produces red cells, white cells, and platelets. At birth all marrow is red; later fat tissue converts part of it to yellow marrow.

A.q: What roles do fibrocartilage and articular cartilage play?
options: Fibro: lubricates; articular: binds bones, limits mobility
Fibro: binds bones, limits mobility; articular: lubricates
Both: generate blood cells in the medullary cavity
Both: store minerals that shape the skeleton
A.explain: Fibrocartilage attaches bone to bone and limits joint mobility; articular cartilage lubricates surfaces for articulation. Neither makes blood or stores minerals.

A.q: Which function belongs to the muscular system rather than to the skeletal system?
A.explain: Producing heat by contraction is a muscular function. Storing minerals, providing attachment, and hemopoiesis are skeletal.

A.q: Which plane divides the body vertically into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions?
A.explain: The coronal or frontal plane is the vertical plane that divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions. The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left portions, the transverse plane divides it into upper and lower portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which plane divides the body vertically into right and left portions?
A.explain: The sagittal or median plane is the vertical plane that divides the body into right and left portions. The coronal plane divides the body into front and back portions, the transverse plane divides it into upper and lower portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which plane divides the body horizontally into upper and lower portions?
A.explain: The transverse or horizontal plane is the plane that divides the body into upper and lower portions. The coronal plane divides the body into front and back portions, the sagittal plane divides it into right and left portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which cell type is the specialized connective tissue cell that forms the skeleton?
A.explain: The osteocyte is the specialized connective tissue cell that forms the skeleton. The chondrocyte is a cartilage cell, the myocyte is a muscle cell, and the fibroblast is a connective tissue cell of fibers rather than of bone.

A.q: The pectoral and pelvic girdles share which structural feature?
options: Ball and socket joints supporting limbs
Flat bones forming the chest cage walls
Irregular bones forming the spinal column
A.explain: Both girdles are ball and socket joints encircling bone to support the limbs. The chest cage, spine, and sesamoid bones are other structures.

A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean muscle?
A.explain: My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o are the three interchangeable spellings of the muscle combining form, seen in myoma, myositis, and muscular. Sarc/o, Fibr/o, and Ton/o mean flesh, fiber, and tone or tension, none of which is muscle. Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint, and Chondr/o means cartilage. Myel/o means bone marrow or spinal cord, Oste/o means bone, and Crani/o means skull.

A.q: Which pair of combining forms both mean joint?
A.explain: Arthr/o and Articul/o both mean joint, as in arthrodynia and articulus. Chondr/o means cartilage and Oste/o means bone; My/o and Muscul/o mean muscle; Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o mean vertebra.

A.q: Which combining form means cartilage or gristle?
A.explain: Chondr/o means cartilage or gristle, as in chondromalacia. Arthr/o means joint, Myel/o means bone marrow or spinal cord, and Oste/o means bone.

A.q: Which pair of combining forms both mean vertebra?
A.explain: Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o both mean vertebra, as in spondylosis and vertebroplasty. Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint, Cost/o and Stern/o mean rib and sternum, and Radi/o and Uln/o mean radius and ulna.

A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean tendon?
A.explain: Ten/o, Tend/o, and Tendin/o are the three combining forms that mean tendon, as in tenotomy and tendinitis. My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o mean muscle; Sarc/o means flesh and Fibr/o means fiber; Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint and Chondr/o means cartilage.

A.q: Which combining form is paired with its correct meaning?
A.explain: Myel/o means bone marrow or spinal cord. Sarc/o means flesh, Fibr/o fiber, and Ton/o tone or tension.

A.q: In the term myeloma, the element myel refers to what?
A.explain: Myel means bone marrow or spinal cord; myeloma is a marrow tumor. The tumor sense comes from -oma, flesh is sarc/o, and muscle is my/o.

A.q: In the term sarcoma, the element sarc refers to what?
A.explain: Sarc means flesh, so sarcoma denotes a tumor of fleshy or soft tissue. Bone marrow is Myel/o, cartilage is Chondr/o, and tendon is Ten/o or Tendin/o.

A.q: The term cervicobrachial joins two combining forms. Which pair of regions does it relate?
options: The chest and the lower back
A.explain: Cervicobrachial is built from Cervic/o (neck) and Brachi/o (arm), so it relates the neck and the arm, as in the cervicobrachial region or the nerves of the brachial plexus emerging from the neck. Rib and skull would need Cost/o and Crani/o. Chest and lower back would need Thorac/o and Lumb/o. Hip and femur would need Pelv/o and Femor/o. None of those forms is present in cervicobrachial.

A.q: In the term thoracolumbar, the element thorac refers to which region?
A.explain: Thorac (and its variant Thoracic) means chest, so the thorac element in thoracolumbar names the chest region, while the lumbar element names the lower back. Lower back is the sense of Lumb/o, the other half of the same word, not of thorac. Neck is Cervic/o and hip is Pelv/o, neither of which appears here. Reading thorac as lower back would swap the two regions the compound joins.

A.q: In the term intercostal, the element cost refers to what?
A.explain: Cost means rib, so intercostal denotes a position between the ribs. Sternum is Stern/o, vertebra is Spondyl/o or Vertebr/o, and skull is Crani/o.

A.q: What does the term craniotomy mean?
options: Removal of part of the skull
A.explain: Craniotomy is crani/o + -tomy: incision into the skull. Removal is craniectomy, inflammation cranitis, and a record a craniogram.

A.q: What does the term dactylitis mean?
A.explain: Dactylitis is built from Dactyl/o (digit) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a digit. Pain would use -dynia, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term chondromalacia mean?
A.explain: Chondromalacia is built from Chondr/o (cartilage) and -malacia (softening), so it denotes softening of cartilage. Inflammation would use -itis, surgical removal would use -ectomy, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term arthrodynia mean?
A.explain: Arthrodynia is built from Arthr/o (joint) and -dynia (pain), so it denotes pain in a joint. Inflammation would use -itis, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term osteoarthrotomy mean?
options: Incision into a bone and a joint
Inflammation of a bone and a joint
A record of a bone and a joint
Softening of a bone and a joint
A.explain: Osteoarthrotomy is built from Oste/o (bone), Arthr/o (joint), and -tomy (incision), so it denotes incision into a bone and a joint. Inflammation would use -itis, a record would use -gram, and softening would use -malacia.

A.q: What does the term spondylosis mean?
options: Surgical removal of a vertebral bone
A.explain: Spondylosis is spondyl/o + -osis: a stiff, immobile condition of the vertebrae. Inflammation is spondylitis and removal is vertebrectomy.

A.q: What does the term tenotomy mean?
A.explain: Tenotomy is built from Ten/o (tendon) and -tomy (incision), so it denotes incision into a tendon. Surgical removal would use -ectomy, inflammation would use -itis, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term tendinitis mean?
A.explain: Tendinitis is built from Tendin/o (tendon) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a tendon, as in wrist tendinitis. Pain would use -dynia, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term dystonia mean?
A.explain: Dystonia is built from the prefix dys- (abnormal) and Ton/o (tone or tension) with -ia (condition), so it denotes abnormal tone or tension, usually of muscle. Pain would use -dynia, inflammation would use -itis, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term pelvimetry mean?
A.explain: Pelvimetry is built from Pelv/i (pelvis) and -metry (measurement), so it denotes measurement of the pelvis. A record would use -gram, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical repair would use -plasty.

A.q: What does the term pelvofemoral mean?
options: Pertaining to the pelvis and the femur
Pertaining to the pelvis and the sternum
Pertaining to the pelvis and the skull
Pertaining to the pelvis and the rib
A.explain: Pelvofemoral is built from Pelv/o (pelvis) and Femor/o (femur) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the pelvis and the femur. The sternum, skull, and rib are named by Stern/o, Crani/o, and Cost/o, none of which appears here.

A.q: What does the term radioulnar mean?
options: Pertaining to the radius and the ulna
Pertaining to the ribs and the sternum
Pertaining to the femur and the tibia
Pertaining to the carpal and the tarsal bones
A.explain: Radioulnar is built from Radi/o (radius) and Uln/o (ulna) with -ar (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the radius and the ulna. The ribs and sternum are Cost/o and Stern/o, the femur and tibia are Femor/o and Tibi/o, and the carpal and tarsal bones are Carp/o and Tars/o.

A.q: What does the term sternocostal mean?
options: Pertaining to the sternum and the ribs
Pertaining to the sternum and the skull
Pertaining to the sternum and the pelvis
Pertaining to the sternum and the vertebra
A.explain: Sternocostal is built from Stern/o (sternum) and Cost/o (rib) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the sternum and the ribs. The skull, pelvis, and vertebra are named by Crani/o, Pelv/o, and Spondyl/o, none of which appears here.

A.q: What does the term myoma mean?
A.explain: Myoma is my/o + -oma: a tumor of muscle tissue. Inflammation is myositis, pain myalgia, and softening myomalacia.

A.q: What does the term myositis mean?
A.explain: Myositis is built from Myos/o (muscle) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of muscle tissue. A tumor would use -oma (myoma), pain would use -dynia, and softening would use -malacia.

A.q: What does the term fibrocartilage mean?
options: Fibrous cartilage binding bone to bone
Elastic cartilage shaping the outer ear
Fibrous cartilage forming the nasal tip
A.explain: Fibrocartilage is cartilage made of fibrous tissue that attaches bones to other bones. Articular cartilage lines joints and elastic cartilage shapes the ear.

A.q: What does the term brachioplasty mean?
A.explain: Brachioplasty is built from Brachi/o (arm) and -plasty (surgical repair), so it denotes surgical repair of the arm. Inflammation would use -itis, pain would use -dynia, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term femoral mean?
A.explain: Femoral is built from Femor/o (femur) and -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the femur. The rib, skull, and vertebra are named by Cost/o, Crani/o, and Spondyl/o.

A.q: What does the term lumbar mean?
A.explain: Lumbar means pertaining to the loin or lower back. Chest is thoracic, neck is cervical, and arm is brachial.

A.q: What does the term fascial mean?
options: Pertaining to fascia, a connective band
Pertaining to fascia, a muscle cord to bone
Pertaining to fascia, a joint between bones
Pertaining to fascia, a contractile tissue
A.explain: Fascial means pertaining to fascia, a band of connective tissue. A cord joining muscle to bone is a tendon, a joint between bones is an articulation, and contractile tissue is muscle.

A.q: What does the term articulus mean?
A.explain: Articulus comes from Articul/o, which means joint, so it denotes a joint. Cartilage is Chondr/o, tendon is Ten/o, and muscle is My/o.

A.q: What does the term osteocyte mean?
A.explain: Osteocyte is built from Oste/o (bone) and -cyte (cell), so it denotes a cell of bone tissue. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term medullary cavity mean?
options: The central space within a bone that contains marrow
The gristle-like covering on the joint surfaces of a bone
The tight solid tissue forming the exterior of a bone
The mesh-like tissue filling the interior of a bone
A.explain: The medullary cavity is the central space within a bone that contains marrow. The gristle-like covering on joint surfaces is articular cartilage, the tight solid exterior tissue is compact bone, and the mesh-like interior tissue is spongy or cancellous bone.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the pectoral girdle?
options: Encircles upper limb; supports the arm
Encircles lower limb; supports the leg
A.explain: The pectoral girdle encircles the upper limb, with ball and socket joints supporting the arm. The pelvic girdle supports the leg.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the pelvic girdle?
options: Encircles upper limb; supports the arm
Encircles lower limb; supports the leg
Forms U-shaped bone at tongue base
A.explain: The pelvic girdle encircles the lower limb and supports the leg. The pectoral girdle supports the arm and the hyoid sits at the tongue base.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Arthr/o and Articul/o both mean joint, as in arthrodynia and articulus. Chondr/o means cartilage or gristle, as in chondromalacia. My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o all mean muscle, as in myoma, myositis, and muscular. Sarc/o means flesh, as in sarcoma. Fibr/o means fiber, as in fibrocartilage. Ton/o means tone or tension, as in dystonia. The paired forms on the left are synonym spellings or closely related forms, so each left entry maps to a single right entry.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Brachi/o means arm, as in brachioplasty. Cervic/o means neck, as in cervicobrachial. Crani/o means skull, as in craniotomy. Dactyl/o means digit, as in dactylitis. Fasci/o means fascia, the band of connective tissue seen in fascial and in the fascial band around muscle fibers. Femor/o means femur, as in femoral. Each form pairs with exactly one structure, and the example terms show the same pairing in use.

A.q: Match each further combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Cost/o means rib, as in intercostal. Lumb/o means the loin or lower back, as in lumbar and thoracolumbar. Oste/o means bone, as in osteoarthrotomy. Pelv/i and Pelv/o are the two spellings for the hip bone or pelvic cavity, as in pelvimetry and pelvofemoral. Radi/o and Uln/o name the two forearm bones, the radius and the ulna, jointly seen in radioulnar. Stern/o means the sternum or breastbone, as in sternocostal. The paired forms on the left are synonym spellings or a natural anatomical pair, so each left entry maps to a single right entry.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.
A.explain: Myel/o means bone marrow or the spinal cord, as in myeloma and leukomyelopathy. Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o both mean vertebra, as in spondylosis and vertebroplasty. Ten/o, Tend/o, and Tendin/o all mean tendon, as in tenotomy and tendinitis. Thorac/o and Thoracic/o mean chest, as in thoracolumbar and thoracicoabdominal. Orth/o means straight, as in orthopedic. Patell/o means the kneecap, or patella.

A.q: Match each term to its meaning.
A.explain: Arthrodynia is joint pain, chondromalacia cartilage softening, craniotomy skull incision, dactylitis digit inflammation, intercostal between the ribs, and osteoarthrotomy incision into bone and joint.

A.q: Match each remaining term to its meaning.
A.explain: Spondylosis is stiff, immobile vertebrae; tenotomy tendon incision; tendinitis tendon inflammation; dystonia abnormal tone; pelvimetry pelvic measurement; pelvofemoral pertaining to pelvis and femur.

A.q: Match each further term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: Fibrous tissue binding bone to bone

A.explain: Radioulnar is radius and ulna, sternocostal sternum and ribs, myoma a muscle tumor, myositis muscle inflammation, fibrocartilage fibrous tissue binding bone to bone, and cervicobrachial neck and arm.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the thoracic cage?
options: Axial; ribs and sternum enclosing chest
Axial; U-shaped bone at tongue base
A.explain: The thoracic cage is axial skeleton, formed by the ribs and sternum, enclosing the chest. The hyoid is the U-shaped bone at the tongue base.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the vertebral column?
A.explain: The vertebral column is axial skeleton forming the central axis of the body. The thoracic cage encloses the chest.

A.q: How do the hyoid and the laryngeal skeleton differ?
options: Hyoid: U-shaped tongue-base bone; larynx: cartilage framework
Hyoid: cartilage framework; larynx: U-shaped tongue-base bone
Hyoid: chest breastbone; larynx: foot heel bone
Hyoid: knee cap; larynx: shoulder blade
A.explain: The hyoid is the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue; the laryngeal skeleton is the cartilage framework of the voice box.

A.q: Orth/o and ped/o are joined to build one musculoskeletal term. Which pairing of meanings and term is correct?
options: Orth/o means straight and ped/o means foot, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means foot and ped/o means straight, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means bone and ped/o means child, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means mouth and ped/o means muscle, forming muscular.
A.explain: Orth/o means straight and ped/o means foot, and the two combine to form orthopedic. The line that assigns foot to Orth/o and straight to ped/o swaps the two forms inside the same term. Orth/o does not mean bone, and the foot sense of ped/o is the one used in orthopedic, so the line that pairs bone with child misses the straight sense and the foot sense. Mouth and muscle are not the senses of Orth/o and ped/o, and muscular is built from muscul/o, not from this pair.

A.q: What does the term myalgia mean?
A.explain: Myalgia is built from My/o (muscle) and -algia (pain), so it denotes pain in a muscle. Pain in a bone would use Oste/o, as in ostealgia. Inflammation of a muscle is myositis, built with -itis. Softening of a muscle would use -malacia, not -algia.

A.q: Which pairing names the breastbone and the combining form used to build terms for it?
options: Sternum, built with the combining form stern/o
Chest wall, built with the combining form thorac/o
Forearm bone, built with the combining form uln/o
Upper arm, built with the combining form brachi/o
A.explain: The breastbone is the sternum, and terms for it are built with stern/o, as in sternocostal and sternalgia. Thorac/o names the chest, not the breastbone itself. Uln/o names the ulna, a forearm bone. Brachi/o names the arm, not the breastbone.

A.q: Which term marks the end of a limb farthest from its point of origin?
options: Distal, away from the origin of the structure
Proximal, near the origin of the structure
Medial, close to the midline of the body
Lateral, toward the side and away from midline
A.explain: Distal marks a point away from the origin or beginning of a structure, so it is the end farthest from that origin. Proximal is the opposite: near the origin, not farthest from it. Medial means close to the midline and does not measure distance from an origin. Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline, and likewise does not mark the far end of a limb.

A.q: What is the imaginary line that runs through the center of the body called?
options: The axis, the central line itself
Medial, a position close to that line
Lateral, a position toward the side
Distal, a point away from an origin
A.explain: The axis is the imaginary line that runs through the center of the body. Medial names a position close to that line, not the line itself. Lateral names a position toward the side, away from the line. Distal names a point away from the origin of a structure and is not the central line.

A.q: Which term names movement away from the midline of the body?
A.explain: Abduction is movement away from the midline of the body. Adduction is the opposite movement, toward the midline. Flexion is bending that decreases the angle at a joint, and extension is straightening that increases that angle. Neither flexion nor extension is defined by direction relative to the midline.

A.q: What does the term sternalgia mean?
A.explain: Sternalgia is built from Stern/o (sternum) and -algia (pain), so it denotes pain in the sternum, the breastbone. Pain in a tendon would use Ten/o or Tendin/o, as in tenalgia. Inflammation of the sternum would use -itis. Excision of the sternum would use -ectomy.

A.explain: Ulna is a long bone of the forearm on the medial side, in the appendicular skeleton, and its combining form is Uln/o. Ulnna, Ulnea, and Ulnar are not the bone name (ulnar is the adjective). It is not a short, flat, or irregular bone. It is not axial. A.q: Which function belongs to the skeleton and is not a function of muscle contraction?
A.explain: Support and shape are skeletal functions. Locomotion, heat, and limb movement come from muscle contraction.

A.q: Which statement about bone tissue is correct?
options: Bone is a dead mineral cast.
Bone is only a nerve tract.
A.explain: Bone is a living structure. It is not a dead mineral cast, not a liquid tissue, and not only a nerve tract. Osteocytes are the specialized connective tissue cells that form it.

A.q: Which marrow is paired with its correct product?
options: Red: blood cells; yellow: fat, cartilage, bone
Yellow: blood cells; red: fat, cartilage, bone
Both: blood cells only, no fat
Both: fat only, no blood cells
A.explain: Red marrow forms blood cells; yellow marrow is tied to fat, cartilage, and bone production.

A.q: Which function is shared by the skeleton and the muscles?
A.explain: Protecting internal organs is listed for both the skeleton and the muscles, so it is the shared function. Hemopoiesis in red marrow is skeletal. Storing minerals in bone tissue is skeletal. Producing body heat through contraction is muscular.

A.q: Ten/o, tend/o, and tendin/o mean tendon. Which sense is paired with that structure?
A.explain: Tendon is paired with the sense to stretch. To soften is the sense of -malacia, to break is not the tendon gloss, and to record is the sense of -gram. Tenotomy is an incision into a tendon, and tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon.

A.q: What does the term thoracicoabdominal mean?
options: Pertaining to the chest and the abdomen
Pertaining to the chest and the lower back
Pertaining to the neck and the arm
Pertaining to the pelvis and the femur
A.explain: Thoracicoabdominal is built from Thoracic/o (chest) and the abdomen, so it means pertaining to the chest and the abdomen. Chest and lower back is thoracolumbar. Neck and arm is cervicobrachial. Pelvis and femur is pelvofemoral.

A.q: In cervical myelopathy, the element myel refers to what?
A.explain: Myel/o means bone marrow or the spinal cord, so in cervical myelopathy the myel element names the spinal cord. Muscle is My/o or Muscul/o. Flesh is Sarc/o. Tendon is Ten/o or Tendin/o. Myeloma uses the same form for a bone-marrow tumor.
